extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of humor theory, comic artists, playwrights, and literary/philosophical scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic criteria for what makes things comic: a philosophical account of laughter focused on form vs. life, mechanisation, repetition, disguise, and the transformation of persons into things. Useful for critics, comic creators, and theorists seeking principled guidance on producing or analysing comic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic as rigidity vs gracefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic arises when the living soul's suppleness is thwarted by matter; where gracefulness is replaced by obstinate, machine‑like resistance, producing rigid, stereotyped attitudes (permanent grimaces, petrified movements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comic partakes of rigidness rather than mere ugliness: look for contrast between an imagined inner mobility and an externally fixed, mechanical form. Examples: faces frozen into a grimace that becomes its own caricature; bodies whose movements are petrified. Scoring note: stronger contrast (more obvious resistance of matter to soul) → stronger comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitudes/gestures laughable in proportion to mechanical suggestion
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The attitudes, gestures and movements of the human body are laughable in exact proportion as that body reminds us of a mere machine.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A drawing, actor, or speaker that clearly but subtly suggests a jointed puppet will be comic. Two necessary conditions: (1) clarity of suggestion so we distinctly perceive a mechanism, and (2) subtlety so the person still appears living. Examples: caricatured drawings that make a person read as a puppet; a public speaker with an automatic recurring gesture. Anti‑pattern: purely borrowed comic context (textual gag) without inherent mechanical suggestion will be less effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition / automatism produces laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: A movement or gesture that repeats identically makes us laugh because it reveals automatism established within life — the gesture becomes mechanical and predictable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition that can be anticipated by the audience converts living action into mechanism. Imitation amplifies this because it exposes the mechanical uniformity. Parodic device: deflect a repeated gesture toward a simple mechanical occupation (sawing wood, striking an anvil) to make its mechanistic nature explicit. Scoring: more regular, expected repetition → stronger comic response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation exposes mechanisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Gestures that never seemed laughable become so when imitated, because imitation highlights their mechanical uniformity and the loss of individual liveliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation functions as a diagnostic: if a gesture is repeatable and imitable, it betrays automatism. Use imitation in performance to reveal the ludicrous element. Note: imitation that merely mocks without revealing underlying automatism is weaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deflection to a mechanical occupation intensifies comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Even without changing a gesture’s form, suggesting it belongs to a simple mechanical task (sawing, tugging a bell‑rope) makes the gesture feel intentionally mechanical and therefore funnier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody favours such mechanical reinterpretations. When creating or analysing parody, explicitly map gestures to mundane mechanical acts to heighten the comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity and absolute uniformity (marionette effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: When several people act in uniform, simultaneously striking the same attitudes, we think of marionettes or invisible threads and perceive a mechanical, puppet‑like scene which is highly comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choreographing groups in strict unison or staging multiple identical characters increases the impression of machinery and thus comic power. Example: chorus of actors making identical gestures; synchronized clown routines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage devices derive humour from suggestion of clockwork arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic devices such as periodic repetition of words/scenes, systematic inversion, geometric progression of misunderstandings, etc., owe their force to presenting human events as an obvious clockwork arrangement while preserving an outward aspect of probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwrights and comedians should aim to construct sequences that feel mechanised yet plausible enough to keep the 'suppleness of life' visible. Overly implausible or random devices that fail to suggest systematic mechanism will miss this source of comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disguise and masquerade reveal latent comic quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Anything perceived as disguise (garment, altered appearance, or what imagination treats as artificially applied) becomes comic because it draws attention to the surface/form separated from the living individual beneath.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic effect emerges when continuity/custom deadens awareness and then a disruption or unfamiliar disguise brings the form into focus. Examples: archaic fashions suddenly worn, unexpected changes of hair or complexion (text uses historical examples). Caution: cultural and ethical sensitivity required when discussing race/appearance — the text analyses imaginative perception (e.g., thinking of colour as 'paint') rather than endorsing prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity/custom masks comic potential; disruption revives it
rubrics_metrics.description: Many things are objectively comic (de jure) but not comic in practice (de facto) because habit and custom deaden the comic quality; a sudden dissolution of continuity is needed to revive it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprise or contrast alone do not suffice; they must reveal an underlying mechanical/masquerade relation. In comic creation, break habituation strategically (anachronism, sudden costume change) to surface the latent comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formality/ceremony vs. matter (ceremony as puppet‑like)
rubrics_metrics.description: When attention is fixed on the ceremonial form or formula rather than the substantive matter it serves, those participating appear puppet‑like and comic. Ceremonies and official formalities contain latent comic elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expose ceremonial elements out of their serious context to generate laughter (e.g., prize distribution, court ritual). Examples: customs officers asking survivors if they have anything to declare; parliamentary or judicial formality becoming the focus. Scoring: the more detached the form is from its serious purpose, the funnier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human regulation/pedantry as comic (artifice usurping nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: The substitution of artificial regulation or pedantic routine for natural laws or ends (administration treating life as business routine) is comic: art pretends to outdo nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirise bureaucratic or pedantic claims that treat rules as natural law. Example: a philosopher saying 'experience is in the wrong' to end an argument. Use amplification of rule‑bound thinking to show absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical intrusions when the moral/spiritual is expected
rubrics_metrics.description: Any incident that recalls the physical side of a person at a moment when the moral, intellectual or spiritual is concerned is comic (e.g., sneezing during a pathetic speech, 'he was virtuous and plump').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious in tragic or solemn contexts: any sign of bodily need or awkwardness undermines the intended gravity and converts the scene to comedy. For creators: avoid gratuitous physical details in serious moments if you want to preserve pathos; conversely, such intrusions are a reliable comedic lever.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner replacing matter (profession/form over purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy arises when manner, form, or ritual is elevated above the real purpose (form becomes end in itself): professions that observe form obsessively appear ludicrous (lawyers, doctors, officials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterisation that emphasises ritualized wording, blind observance of rules, or formality over outcome produces comic effect. Authors can pair this with physical overtones (stammering, slow speech) to compound the ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical defects as comic overtones completing intellectual rigidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical quirks (stammering, slow speech, stuttering) serve as overtones that prepare the audience to perceive intellectual ossification or professional rigidity — the bodily defect echoes moral or mental stiffness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing comic characters, match a physical speech rhythm or defect to an intellectual foible to create coherent comic resonance. If absent, actors often invent such traits instinctively. Example: Molière's ridiculous doctors with contrasting speech rhythms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person perceived as a thing (transformation into object)
rubrics_metrics.description: We laugh when a person gives the impression of being a thing — when human figures are suggested to become balls, dolls, wooden dummies, etc.; theatrical sequences that gradually make bodies appear inanimate are comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achieve this by progressive suggestion: repeated falls and rebounds, exaggeration of weight/rigidity, or gradual 'solidifying' imagery. Use staging, rhythm and choreography to create the hallucination of objecthood. Literary devices (rhythm, rhyme, assonance) can lull imagination toward accepting a doll‑like image.
